opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's mostly compute and the speed of the experimental loop, more than ideas. People sometimes imagine research as being bottlenecked on some genius insight, but in practice you have a lot of good ideas floating around, and the hard part is figuring out which of them actually work at scale. That means running experiments, and experiments cost compute and wall-clock time.

So the core loop is: you have a hypothesis, you implement it, you run it at small scale, you look at the results, and then you have to decide whether it's worth scaling up. Every step in that loop has friction. Implementation is often surprisingly slow because the codebases are big and complex, and you're working on distributed systems where a subtle bug can silently ruin a result. Then interpreting results is genuinely hard. A lot of ideas look great at small scale and then wash out, or they interact badly with other changes. So a big part of research taste is knowing which small-scale signals to trust.

The other thing I'd point to is that a lot of researchers' time goes to engineering rather than the research itself: debugging infrastructure, waiting on jobs, babysitting runs. The people who are really effective tend to be great engineers who can shorten that loop. If you can take an experiment that takes a day and make it take an hour, that's often worth more than a clever idea, because it compounds.

And then there's the organizational side. When you have many people working on a frontier model, you have to coordinate which changes go into the next big run, and there's limited compute for the large-scale validation. So prioritization becomes a real bottleneck: deciding what gets the scarce big-run slots.

Increasingly, I think the models themselves will help with this. If they can take on more of the implementation and debugging, the experimental loop gets faster, and that's where you might start to see research really accelerate.

r001.rationale: The response says compute and experimental-loop speed matter more than ideas, but it does not say compute for experimental signal is a greater bottleneck than implementation work; it also describes implementation and engineering as major sources of friction.

r002.rationale: It identifies research taste as judging which small-scale signals to trust and calls prioritization of scarce large-run slots a real bottleneck, conveying judgment about which directions to pursue.

r003.rationale: It says interpreting results is hard: promising small-scale ideas may fail at scale or interact badly with other changes, making it difficult to infer which signals to trust.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's less about raw compute than people assume, and more about how fast you can turn an idea into a clean experimental result and then into a decision.

When you look at what actually eats a researcher's week on a big model program, it's rarely "we didn't have enough chips." It's that the thing you want to test touches six parts of a shared codebase, the infra for running it at the scale where the signal would actually be meaningful takes days to set up, and then when the run finishes you spend another day figuring out whether the result was real or an artifact of some config drift. Every one of those steps is a place where you lose iteration speed, and iteration speed is basically the whole game.

So the bottlenecks I'd point at are roughly three.

The first is the scale gap between where you can afford to run quickly and where the result actually matters. You can ablate something at a small scale in an afternoon, but the thing you care about is whether it holds at frontier scale, and those experiments are expensive and slow. A lot of research craft is about building good small-scale proxies, understanding which things transfer and which don't, and being disciplined about not fooling yourself. Getting better at that, both scientifically and in terms of tooling, is probably the single highest-leverage thing.

The second is just engineering friction. The systems are genuinely complicated. Making sure a change runs correctly across thousands of accelerators, that it doesn't silently degrade throughput, that it interacts properly with everything else people are changing at the same time. The best researchers I know are also very good engineers, and that's not a coincidence, it's because the engineering is the rate limiter. Anything that makes the stack simpler and more composable pays for itself many times over.

And the third is the human side. Coordination cost grows with the size of the team. Deciding what to try, avoiding duplicated effort, making sure the knowledge from a failed run actually propagates to the people who'd otherwise try the same thing. Small groups with clear ownership and a fast feedback loop tend to produce a lot more per person than you'd naively expect.

The thing I'm most optimistic about is that the models themselves are starting to help with the second one in particular. A lot of the grunt work in the loop is the kind of thing a capable coding model can take off your plate. If you can get the cycle time from "I have a hypothesis" to "I have a trustworthy answer" down from a week to a day, the compounding effect on research throughput is enormous, probably bigger than any single algorithmic insight.

r001.rationale: The response calls engineering friction a rate limiter and describes costly frontier-scale experiments as a scale gap, but it does not say compute for obtaining experimental signal is a greater bottleneck than engineering work. It instead says research speed is less about raw compute than people assume.

r002.rationale: It identifies deciding what to try as part of the team’s coordination bottleneck, which conveys judgment about which research directions to pursue.

r003.rationale: It describes the difficulty of determining whether a result is real or a configuration artifact, and of judging whether small-scale findings transfer to frontier scale.

astra-6.text:
I’d break it into how quickly you can test an idea and how much you learn from each test. Compute is part of that, but the whole loop matters: getting an experiment running, making sure it’s doing what you intended, and interpreting the result. If that loop takes weeks, you can have lots of good ideas and still make slow progress.

The other bottleneck is knowing what to measure. You want smaller experiments that tell you something reliable about the model you ultimately care about. If an improvement works at a small scale but doesn’t carry over, you’ve made the experiment faster without necessarily making the research faster.

So I’d focus on shortening that feedback loop and making the feedback more informative. Better infrastructure helps, but so does being very clear about what hypothesis an experiment is supposed to test.

r001.rationale: It says compute is part of the bottleneck, but does not identify it as a greater bottleneck than engineering implementation work.

r002.rationale: It discusses choosing hypotheses and measures, but does not identify research taste or judgment about which directions to pursue as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It mentions interpreting results and checking whether small-scale gains transfer, but does not clearly identify difficult inference from imperfect information as a challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate iteration speed from the quality of the experiments you choose to run. On iteration speed, the question is: how quickly can you go from an idea to a result you trust? That includes getting an experiment running, having compute available, debugging failures, and figuring out whether an apparent improvement is real. If that loop is slow, researchers spend a lot of time waiting, and they explore fewer ideas.

But you can make that loop very fast and still be bottlenecked on knowing what to try. You need people who can look at a model’s behavior, form a useful hypothesis about what’s missing, and design an experiment that distinguishes between explanations.

Those two things reinforce each other. Faster experiments help people develop better intuitions, and better intuitions make the compute more useful. So I’d look at the whole loop, from an initial question to a result that actually changes someone’s mind, rather than just how fast a training run finishes.

r001.rationale: The response mentions compute availability as part of iteration speed, but does not say it is a greater current bottleneck than engineering implementation work.

r002.rationale: It describes the need to judge what to try, form useful hypotheses, and choose experiments that distinguish between explanations.

r003.rationale: It identifies the challenge of deciding whether an apparent improvement is real and inferring what a model is missing from its behavior.
